January 16
Epiphany 2C — The Second Sunday of Epiphany
Colors: green
Isaiah 62:1-5
Psalm 96
1 Cor 12:1-11
Jn 2:1-11
Grace and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ - who did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.


If I had to pick a moment in time when the era of the Old Testament ended, and the New Testament began, I would choose the moment when Jesus turned the water into wine at the Wedding in Cana (John 2:1-11).


    Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in [the Gospel of John]; but these are written so that you may [trust] that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by [trusting] you may have life in his name - John 20:30-31


So St. John tells us.


Of all the things St. John could have told us that Jesus did, he chose seven miracles to teach about who Jesus is. The first of the seven is changing the water to wine at a wedding in Cana.


What, then, is it that causes me to think this is THE MOMENT when the Old Testament comes to end and the New Testament begins? There are two things: the first is the miracle itself and the second is the setting of the miracle. The prophets of the Old Testament use several images to describe what it will be like when the Messiah comes. One of the images used is that of a wedding feast. Another is a ridiculous abundance of wine.


Admittedly not everyone enjoys a wedding feast - mostly men. I am informed by the Long Suffering Mrs. Sutcliffe that women enjoy weddings because of the romance, reminiscing, dancing, and getting dressed up. Oddly, these are the exact reasons why most men do not like weddings. That being said, most men enjoy drinking in the presence of other men, especially when there are women around to look at. This may be an affectation of our current age, but somehow I doubt it.


In the time of Jesus - and throughout most of history for that matter - a wedding feast was THE BIG DEAL and would go on for multiple days. In spite of having to get dressed up (in order to be appropriate arm candy for women), I imagine most men would relish the opportunity to spend several days drinking, eating, and not working, even if they did have to behave themselves.


Although this is an imperfect analogy, we'll go with it for now: The Old Testament era is a bit like getting ready for the banquet, where men are annoyed about showering, shaving, and putting on uncomfortable clothes while women worry about how they look and if every last wisp of hair is properly placed. In the New Testament era the party has begun; there are Swedish meatballs, plenty to drink, and a cookie table. The men are loosening their ties and women are slipping off their uncomfortable shoes and letting the hair fall where it may.  


At the wedding in Cana, they ran out of wine, and this was a major disaster. The wedding in Cana is in danger of failing to be a reflection of the Messianic banquet. When Jesus turns the water into wine, he is changing the water of Old Testament purification into the New Testament celebratory wine and, as such, marks the end of the Old Testament era and the beginning of the New. Apparently, Jesus' disciples see it that way; as St. John records, they trusted Jesus to be the Messiah.


In St. John's Gospel, there are six other signs, and each teaches us something about Jesus and his lordship. At the second sign, an official whose son is ill asks Jesus to heal his boy. Jesus' response is, "unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe" (John 4:48). The official responds with, "Sir, come down before my child dies," whereupon Jesus says, "Go; your son will live." The official leaves, and his son is healed. We learn two things from this sign. The first is the importance of trusting Jesus. Jesus says, *go* and the official goes. The second and perhaps more important lesson is that the REAL signs and wonders of Jesus are his words.


The third sign is where Jesus heals the paralytic, saying, "Get up, take up your bed and walk." Of course, he does. The thing is, Jesus does this on the Sabbath putting himself in the crosshairs of the Pharisees and Seducees. But what we learn is that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath. 


In the fourth sign Jesus feeds 5000 men, plus the women and children. There are clear parallels between Moses and the Jews being fed manna in the desert. Even so, Jesus makes it clear the bread that was eaten in the desert only filled bellies. It was an Old Testament filling. The bread Jesus offers is himself; it is New Testament bread, and it leads to New Testament life.


The fifth sign forms a sort of interlude in the midst of the fourth sign - Jesus walks on the water. The lesson is simple: the Creator of everything is lord of everything. St. John offers Jesus' walking on the Sea of Galilee as proof that Jesus is Lord of everything and affirms what he wrote at the beginning of his gospel, "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:3).


In the 9th chapter, we have the sixth sign where Jesus gives sight to the man who had been blind since birth. In short, this sign affirms that Jesus is the light of the world, again reflecting the first chapter where St. John says


    In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5-6)


Not only does Jesus bring light, but darkness has no power over the light that Jesus brings.


The last of the seven signs is Jesus calling the dead Lazarus out of the grave and back to life. The easy lesson is that Jesus not only has power over darkness, but power over death.


St. John tells us all of these things so that we might come to understand and trust that Jesus, being one with his Father through the Holy Spirit, is God who creates everything that is created and God makes this Creation out of pure love for what He created. Whether or not we love in return does not diminish in the slightest the love God has for his Creation - which, to be clear, includes you. “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31) as St. Paul tells us. He goes on, “For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38-39). How can we disagree?


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always. 
paul+
